verdicts.summary: Lean has an equivalent formula. The display is the definiens of a named property ("g is flat at the radial edge X_e"). The repository has no predicate with that name or shape; it writes the defining formula out wherever it needs it. For the edge weight ζ, the only object for which a numbered result of the paper asserts the property (Theorem 4.6(iv), which itself spells it out as "every radial derivative of ζ vanishes at X_a, X_b"), the Lean formula is the display verbatim: iteratedDeriv n (radialWeight c a b) (exp a) = 0 and ... (exp b) = 0 for every n : ℕ, with LeadingStressWeights.zeta defined as radialWeight (activationTime^2) (leftEdge W) (rightEdge W) and leftEdge/rightEdge the logs of activeLeft/activeRight; n = 0 is included and the η quantifier is vacuous because ζ depends on X only. The η-dependent form of the formula is also stated, in (X, η) coordinates and for every η, for the first-order terminal stress model at the outer edge: stressX_edge_jets gives vanishing of every full Fréchet jet at (exp(y0+3), η), which is more than the pure X-derivatives the paper asks for (profileStress_edge_jets is the same in the edge chart). What I did not find is a jets-vanish statement for the actual leading stress `stress v.profiles F.data.h` at the inner edge X_a; there the repository carries stress_zero_before plus the EdgeFactor identity on 0 < x < width. That concerns the paper's following sentence ("The stress will be flat at both edges") and Theorem 4.6(ii),(iv), not this defining display. NativeDyadicRegularity.FlatAt, which finding B pairs with the display, is a pointwise all-jets predicate used only in NativeDyadicRegularity.lean and InitialDyadicSource.lean for the dyadic faces; I found no use of it at X_a or X_b, so I do not count it as the counterpart, and B's argument recovering mixed jets from pure X-jets is not a step the repository states and is not needed.
